Key issues: Lemma 1's CRT argument — x_k avoids only primes p_1..p_{k-1}, but must avoid all primes dividing a_i. Since a_i for i<n_k contain only primes among p_1..p_{k-1}? Wait, p_k is the k-th smallest prime in P, and n_k is first appearance of p_k — but a_i (i<n_k) could contain primes larger than p_k that appeared earlier. The write-up claims P(a_i) contains only primes among {p_1,...,p_{k-1}} — false in general, larger primes may appear before smaller ones. So Lemma 1's proof is flawed. Actually is Lemma 1 even true? Yes, known result; but proof must handle arbitrary new primes. The construction only handles the case of smallest new prime issue — flawed. Also the inequality "a_{n_k} must be at least p_k, which exceeds L_k for large k" is wrong: L_k = product of first k primes in P, which is bigger than p_k always. Actually claim "x_k ≤ a_{n_k-1} + L_k < a_{n_k}" — justification fails since L_k > p_k typically. So Lemma 1's proof has serious errors.

Lemma 2: minimal hitting sets could also grow (new sets) as F_n grows — actually adding sets can create new minimal hitting sets not subsets of old ones. The claim M_{n+1} ⊆ M_n ∪ ... is sketchy but finiteness of subsets of P* gives stabilization anyway once P finite — since M_n are minimal hitting sets over finite ground set, sequence... actually M_n is not monotone; but since P* finite, infinitely many n have same M? No—could oscillate? Adding sets to F_n: a minimal hitting set for F_{n+1} must hit new set; not monotone. Could alternate infinitely? Ground set finite, families could oscillate? Once a hitting set fails, it stays failing; but new minimal hitting sets appear. Number of possible families finite but sequence needn't be monotone... Actually a set H hits F_n iff it hits every P(a_i). As n grows, more constraints, so set of hitting sets shrinks monotonically. Hence minimal hitting sets: minimal elements of shrinking family — M_n ⊆? Not monotone, but only finitely many changes possible? Minimal hitting sets of a shrinking family can change infinitely? The families are subsets of a finite power set, hitting sets shrink monotonically, so the hitting set family stabilizes after finitely many steps (each new term removes at least one hitting set or nothing; only finitely many sets total). So M_n stabilizes. Fine.

Lemma 3 is handwavy ("as we will show", circular with Lemma 4). Its "proof" is essentially a sketch with admitted gaps ("formalized in Lemma 4", "rigorous pigeonhole argument" asserted). Lemma 5 fine given 3-4. Lemma 6: the claim gcd(x+L,y+L)=gcd(x,y) "when L is multiple of all primes dividing any term" is false generally; also b-sequence satisfying greedy rule unproven. Actually b_n = a_{n+T} - L — does it satisfy the greedy rule from a_1? Not justified, and uniqueness argument flawed: two sequences satisfying the greedy rule with the same a_1 are equal, but need b to satisfy rule with correct initial term and b_1 = a_1 must be shown (b_1 = a_{1+T}-L = a_1 needs conclusion). Circular. So backward propagation is a major gap.

Overall: correct high-level structure, but Lemma 1's proof has a genuine error (claim about primes ordering / bound), Lemma 3 sketchy, Lemma 6 circular/invalid. Substantial progress with major gaps: grade 3-4. I'd say 3.
